name: Rollright Stones
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Rollright Stones are a mythic place in Britain. This ring of tall stones stands where the shires of Oxfordshire and Warwickshire meet. Many tales cling to it. One holds that the stones defeat every attempt to number them. One sharp baker sought to number the stones by resting a single loaf on every rock. He planned to go back, gathered the loaves, and count them that way. The bread never proved enough, or it disappeared as he set each loaf down. Some scholars think the legends grew from an old custom of giving food to the stones. A second tale tells of an invading king. A prophecy said he would govern all of Britain upon first sight of the town of Long Compton. Some of his own knights turned against him while he camped by the stones. Dreading betrayal, the ruler crept away under cover of dark. Before he could climb to a point overlooking Long Compton, a witch crossed his path. She changed the ruler into the rock called the King Stone, and set his murmuring knights into stone beside him. Should the spell someday break, the fallen ruler and his troops will rise and march across England. For the present they rest as rock. The witch endures close by in the shape of an elder tree. Some tell that, under cover of darkness, the stones slip away to a nearby stream to drink. Then, at every midnight, they rouse themselves and move in a dance while the King Stone takes his drink. The circle itself may predate the Celts, but a Celtic hill fort once stood not far off.
